title: Spondylolysis and Spondylolisthesis
case: Case: A 15-year-old fast bowler has 6 weeks of low back pain that is worse when bowling and arching. Rest eases it. No leg symptoms, normal reflexes, tight hamstrings. Single-leg extension on the right reproduces his pain.

Working diagnosis: suspected right-sided pars stress injury (spondylolysis). Plan: stop bowling and other provoking sport, refer for medical imaging, begin pain-free trunk and hip exercises, review with the doctor's findings.

differentials.name: Non-specific mechanical low back pain
differentials.key: No extension-biased provocation, no young athlete pattern

differentials.name: Lumbar facet joint pain
differentials.key: Extension and rotation hurt, similar to pars pain
differentials.next: Treat as mechanical pain; image if young athlete and persisting

differentials.name: Lumbar radiculopathy
differentials.key: Dermatomal leg pain, positive neural tension

differentials.name: Scheuermann disease or other adolescent spine condition

qa: Why is a positive stork test not enough to confirm spondylolysis? Its accuracy is low and other structures can also reproduce the pain, so imaging is needed for confirmation.
Why avoid repeated extension exercises early? They load the area that may be injured and could delay healing.
Why check hamstrings? Tight hamstrings are common in slips and affect pelvic posture and loading.
A 62-year-old with a slip also has leg heaviness on walking. Which chapter do you add? Stenosis (Ch 4), because the leg symptoms point to neurogenic claudication.
The patient asks whether the slipped bone will get worse. What do you say? Most slips stay stable in adults, but this cannot be promised. Explain the monitoring plan and when to report new symptoms.

fields.Purpose: Check whether loaded extension reproduces typical pars-related pain
fields.Patient position: Standing on one leg, holding a support if needed
fields.Therapist position: Behind or beside the patient, ready to steady them
fields.Action: The patient stands on one leg, then extends the lumbar spine and rotates slightly toward the standing leg side; hold for a short moment. Repeat on the other leg
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the patient's familiar low back pain on the standing leg side
fields.Supports: Raises suspicion of a pars-related problem
fields.Limits: Reported accuracy is low, and the test can also be positive with other posterior structures such as facet joints. A negative test does not exclude spondylolysis
fields.Common errors: Not reaching full extension; allowing hip instead of spine movement; counting muscle strain pain
fields.Next step: If positive in an adolescent athlete with a suggestive history, arrange medical imaging via referral and restrict provocative activity

fields.Action: Run the thumbs along the spinous processes of L3 to S1 and feel for a step
fields.Positive: A palpable step suggests a forward slip
fields.Limits: Soft tissue, body weight and posture can hide or mimic a step; reliability is limited

redFlags.Finding: Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction
redFlags.Immediate action: Stop; hospital the same day (Vol 4 Ch 3)

redFlags.Finding: Child or adolescent with severe pain, visible deformity or gait change
redFlags.Immediate action: Refer to spine specialist; avoid loading

redFlags.Finding: Slip that appears to increase on repeated review

manual.name: Hip and thoracic mobilization
manual.why: May reduce load on the lumbar spine

manual.name: Hamstring and hip flexor soft tissue or stretching
manual.why: Reduces pelvic pull on the lumbar spine

manual.name: Central lumbar mobilization
manual.why: Not preferred at the slipped level
manual.application: If used, gentle low-grade, at adjacent levels
manual.stop: Any increase in symptoms or neurological sign

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: active rehabilitation and load management, not forceful lumbar manual techniques. Avoid high-velocity manipulation and strong extension mobilization at the slipped level because stability is the concern and benefit is unproven.

exercise.Steps: Lying with knees bent, gently tighten the lower abdomen without holding the breath
Lying, lower opposite arm and leg while keeping the back still
Support on elbow and knees, lift hips
Lying, strap around the foot, straighten the leg

exerciseNotes: Avoid early: repeated end-range extension, heavy loaded extension and twisting, and for young athletes the sport activity that provokes pain until reviewed.

Young athletes: activity restriction and bracing in some cases are used for suspected active stress injuries, but the optimal approach and the benefit of bracing are debated. Return to sport is graded by pain, function and imaging advice from the medical team. No fixed number of weeks is given here.

modalities.name: Lumbar brace
modalities.comment: Used selectively in young patients with stress injury

pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Adolescent or young athlete with extension-related low back pain and a suggestive test? Yes: working diagnosis is possible spondylolysis. Restrict provocative activity and refer for imaging.
Older adult with back pain and walking-related leg symptoms? Yes: consider degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis (Ch 4).
No nerve signs, stable, mild to moderate pain? Yes: start conservative care.
Persistent disabling symptoms, progressive slip or neurological deficit? Yes: surgical opinion through a doctor.
Visit 1: screen flags and CES, explain what the finding means and does not mean, advise on activity changes.
Early: reduce provoking activities, begin pain-free trunk and hip exercises.
Middle: progress strength, flexibility, movement control and sport or work drills.
